newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Yugoslav spring sowing about complete, near plan.
newsitem.headline: Yugoslav spring sowing about complete, near plan.

text.p: Spring sowing in Yugoslavia was completed on 2.304 million hectares by May 19, or 96 percent of the planned area of 2.396 million ha, the Yugoslav Chamber of Commerce Agriculture Committee said in its latest report.

"The weather in the last days of May and first days of June was not favourable for crops, but better conditions can be expected with alternate dry and moist spells forecast in the coming weeks," committee president Miroslav Jovanovic said.

By May 19, the area under foodgrains was 145,000 ha or 34 percent above the 108,200 ha planned, primarily due to favourable weather during sowing and a larger area sown to barley for brewing, the report said.

Despite a late start due to bad weather, maize was sown on 1.435 million ha, slightly above the 1.406 million ha target. The quality of the maize plants is variable and weeds are growing fast. Measures are also needed to protect the crop from maize beetles which are spreading in the Srem and Banat regions in Vojvodina, the report said.
Poor weather was blamed for the failure to meet other crop targets.

Sugarbeet was the most below target with just 58,171 ha out of a planned 100,000 ha sown. Sugarbeet had to be resown on some 20,000 ha in late April and early May after cold weather and frost damaged emerging crops.
Industry sources feared the final figure would be even lower since weeding and cultivation of re-sown areas has not been completed yet.
"The first sowing was unsucessful and we can expect several thousand hectares more to fail," said Petrasin Otasevic of Jugosecer sugar producers association.

Some 85 percent or 170,222 ha of a planned 200,000 ha were sown to sunflowers but acreage can be expected to increase slightly, the chamber of commerce report said. But sowing was done on inadequately prepared soil so crop growth is variable.
Soybean was planted on 69,867 ha or 80 percent of the planned 80,000 ha and the condition of the crop is good.
But industry sources warned that these results could not be preserved without finance.

"We have managed to complete this job despite extremely difficult conditions and without credits but the basic problem of how to finance agricultural production remains," said Bogdan Obradovic, a Serbian Chamber of Commerce official.

In an effort to ease the financial burden on farmers, the government has postponed farmers' taxes and enabled exchange of commodities for machinery through the Commodity Reserve Agency but producers said this was not enough.
The government did not pay farmers for last year's crops until late March, while most sugar refineries have not repaid primary producers yet.
"Refineries will not be able to repay producers because they have neither the funds nor the stocks to do so," Otasevic said.

Several of Yugoslavia's 15 sugar refineries are bankrupt, six have not paid electricity bills for last year and in the five years since sanctions were imposed on Yugoslavia there has been no capacity overhaul, he added.
Unless measures are taken soon, sugarbeet farmers will be deterred from sowing at all, Otasevic said. --Belgrade newsroom +381 11 222 4305
